questions.q: A film uses a narrator to explain a historical argument over archival footage. Which mode is it mainly in?
questions.explain: Direct address making a case is expository.

questions.q: A filmmaker follows a school for a year with no narration, no interviews and no music. Which mode?
questions.explain: Watching events unfold with the filmmaker unobtrusive.

questions.q: A director puts herself on camera interviewing and arguing with her subjects. Which mode?
questions.explain: The filmmaker's interaction becomes part of the film.

questions.q: A film keeps showing the crew, the editing table and the audience watching. Which mode?
questions.explain: Reflexive documentaries draw attention to how documentaries are made and read.

questions.q: Are Nichols's modes a sequence, from early to advanced?
choices: Yes: poetic came first and performative is the most developed
No: they overlap in time and films mix them
Yes, but only for American films
questions.explain: Vertov's reflexive film dates from 1929; the modes are lenses, not stages.

questions.q: What does 'the creative treatment of actuality' highlight?
choices: That documentary must not be edited
That fiction and documentary are identical
Real material is selected and shaped into an argument
That actuality footage is always objective
questions.explain: The phrase, attributed to Grierson, names the form's central tension.

questions.q: A documentary editor has 200 hours of footage and no script. What's the most useful first step?
choices: Cut chronologically and see what happens
Build a paper edit: find the protagonist, question and turns from transcripts
questions.explain: Documentary structure is usually found in the edit.

questions.q: Why is staging a scene a bigger betrayal in an observational film than in a reflexive one?
choices: Observational films promise you're seeing life as it happened
It isn't; staging is equally fine in both
questions.explain: Each mode makes a different promise; breaking it silently breaks trust.

ideas: Documentary is best understood not as a window on reality but as a voice making an argument with real sounds and images.
Documentaries can be sorted into overlapping modes, such as observational, participatory and reflexive, according to how they address the viewer.
Each way of making a documentary makes a different promise to its audience about how the footage relates to reality.
